client: I've been paralyzed with anxiety ever since I failed those two exams last semester. I can't stop thinking about how it's going to affect my graduation timeline, and I'm terrified I won't be able to catch up. I know I should be studying now, but the fear just makes me freeze up and avoid everything.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a heavy weight of worry and self-doubt, and I can hear the urgency and distress in your voice as you share this. Let’s take a moment to step back and examine the evidence—is it certain that failing those exams will derail everything, or might there be other ways to move forward?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess it’s not *certain* it’ll derail everything, but it feels like it will. I keep replaying worst-case scenarios in my head, like having to retake classes or falling behind my peers. It’s hard to imagine any other way forward when I’m stuck in this panic. I don’t know how to stop spiraling.
therapist: I hear the exhaustion in your voice as you describe being trapped in these worst-case scenarios—it sounds like the panic has drained your energy to the point where even imagining alternatives feels impossible right now. Would it help to unpack one of those scenarios together, to see if we can find even one small crack in that certainty that everything is ruined?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess we could try unpacking one scenario, but I’m not sure it’ll help. For example, I keep thinking I’ll have to retake classes, which means I’ll graduate late and fall behind everyone else. Even if that’s not certain, it still feels like a huge failure, and I don’t know how to cope with that.
therapist: Your voice sounds both resigned and weary as you describe this fear of falling behind—like the weight of potential failure has worn you down. Let’s gently challenge that assumption: what makes graduating on time the only measure of success, rather than something like persistence or learning how to navigate setbacks?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I never thought about it that way, but I guess I've always tied my worth to hitting milestones perfectly on schedule. My parents and professors all emphasize "staying on track," so falling behind feels like admitting I'm not good enough. But hearing you say "persistence" as success makes my chest feel a little lighter, even if I don't fully believe it yet.
therapist: It’s clear how much pressure you’ve been carrying from external expectations, and I can hear both the tension and a glimmer of relief in your voice as you begin to consider a different perspective. Let’s explore this further—what would it mean to redefine success for yourself, separate from the timeline others have set for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Redefining success feels like a huge shift, and honestly, it’s scary. I’ve spent so long measuring myself by grades and timelines that I don’t even know what success would look like outside of that. Part of me wants to try, but another part is worried I’ll just disappoint myself—and everyone else—even more.
therapist: I hear the fear and conflict in your voice—this idea of redefining success seems to shake something fundamental for you, and that uncertainty comes through so clearly. It makes sense that stepping away from familiar measures like grades and timelines would feel disorienting; would it help to start small, perhaps by naming just one thing you value about yourself that has nothing to do with academic achievement?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: Hmm, I guess I do value that I’m a pretty loyal friend. I’m always there for my friends when they need someone to listen or lean on. But it feels strange to focus on that when academics feel like the “real” measure of success in my life. I’m not sure how that helps with the panic over failing exams.
therapist: I notice a shift in your tone—there’s a quiet warmth when you talk about being a loyal friend, even though your words still carry hesitation about whether that "counts." That disconnect tells me how deeply academics have defined your self-worth. What if we explored how bringing that same loyalty and care you show others *to yourself* might change how you view this academic setback?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That's... actually really hard to imagine. I'm so used to beating myself up over mistakes that the idea of showing myself the same kindness I'd show a friend feels almost wrong. Like, if I go easy on myself, won't I just slack off even more? The panic to perform is what's kept me going all these years.
therapist: I hear the conflict in your voice—the way it tightens when you talk about self-kindness feeling "wrong," like loosening that grip on yourself might send everything tumbling. That fear makes so much sense when panic has been your fuel for so long. But let me ask: has that constant pressure *actually* helped you perform, or has it left you frozen and exhausted, like you described earlier?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: You’re right—the pressure hasn’t really helped me perform. If anything, it’s made me feel more overwhelmed and stuck. But the idea of letting go of that panic is terrifying because it feels like I’ll lose control completely. What if I just stop caring altogether?
therapist: Your voice sounds so weary and hesitant as you say this—like you’re standing at the edge of letting go but terrified the ground will disappear beneath you. It makes perfect sense that this panic has felt like a safety net, even as it paralyzes you. Could we explore a middle ground, where "letting go" might simply mean treating yourself with the same patience you’d offer a struggling friend, rather than abandoning care altogether?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I could try treating myself with more patience, but it feels unnatural, like I’m faking it. I’m so used to being harsh with myself that kindness almost feels like cheating. But maybe if I start small, like not yelling at myself for missing a study session, it could help. Still, I’m worried it’ll feel forced or ineffective.
therapist: I hear the uncertainty and discomfort in your voice—like you’re stepping into unfamiliar territory and it feels shaky and awkward. That’s completely normal when trying something new, especially when it goes against habits you’ve held for so long. Starting small, like you’ve suggested, is a great first step—what if we reframe "faking it" as simply practicing a new skill, one that might feel strange at first but could grow more natural over time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That makes sense, but I'm still skeptical. Practicing self-kindness feels like trying to write with my non-dominant hand - frustrating and unnatural. Maybe if I think of it as an experiment rather than something I have to get "right," it would take some pressure off. But I worry I'll just forget to do it when I'm in the middle of panicking about school.
therapist: Your voice still carries that edge of frustration and doubt—I can hear how much this experiment challenges your instincts, even as you're willing to try. That tension makes complete sense when you're used to pushing yourself so hard. Would it help to brainstorm some gentle reminders or cues for those panicked moments, so this new approach doesn't get lost when you need it most?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
